rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero prior information about which design choices (modality, encoder, profile strategy, aggregation, fusion) matter or interact. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most standard baseline in the design space. It establishes a clean performance floor using a well-understood dimensionality reduction (PCA-2000) on the RNA modality alone, with no confounding from image processing, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, the first experiment should maximize interpretability of all subsequent comparisons. Every later configuration can be framed as 'what does adding X (image, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, fusion, alternative encoder) contribute relative to this baseline?' Starting with the simplest, most established configuration avoids conflating multiple novel design choices in one run and gives the clearest signal for the next round of targeted ablations.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), the dominant uncertainty is whether adding image information in a multimodal setup meaningfully improves over the RNA-only baseline. Config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the minimal, clean extension of config_001: it keeps the same RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and profile setting (singleprofile) while adding a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion. This isolates the effect of multimodal fusion as the single changed factor, making the comparison to config_001 directly interpretable. If config_016 substantially outperforms config_001, it validates the multimodal direction and justifies subsequent experiments exploring better image encoders, multiprofile aggregation, and fusion strategies within the multimodal family. If it does not, it tells us the bottleneck lies elsewhere (e.g., RNA encoder quality or profile representation), redirecting the search toward RNA-side improvements. Under a tight budget, resolving this fundamental modality question first maximizes the information gained per experiment and prevents wasting runs on a suboptimal branch.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.527 acc / 0.510 F1, a meaningful +4.2% improvement over rna-only baseline (config_001), confirming that image features add value. However, we have only tested one fusion strategy (concat). Uncertainty: We do not know whether weighted fusion could further improve or degrade performance relative to simple concatenation. This experiment (config_017) isolates exactly one variable—changing fusion from concat to weighted—while holding model_setting, profile_setting, RNA encoder, and image encoder identical to config_016. This gives a clean causal read on fusion strategy. Why best next: Under a tight budget, a single-variable comparison against our current best result is the most information-dense experiment. The outcome directly determines whether all future multimodal configurations should default to weighted or concat fusion, effectively halving the remaining search space. It is a low-risk exploitation step that also reduces a key design uncertainty before we invest experiments in larger architectural changes (multiprofile, ViT-L, alternative RNA encoders).

Evidence: Three completed experiments show RNA-only (0.485) and two multimodal variants with ResNet50 (0.527 concat, 0.523 weighted), confirming that adding an image modality improves performance by ~4%. However, we have no image-only baseline, so we cannot decompose whether the multimodal gain comes from complementary information or simply from the image modality being strong on its own. Question tested: config_010 (image-only, single profile, ResNet50) isolates the image contribution. If image-only performs near 0.52, the RNA signal adds little and future effort should focus on image encoders; if it performs much lower (~0.35-0.40), the gain is truly synergistic and fusion strategy becomes critical. Why best next experiment: With only 3 data points, the evidence is sparse and the most important design uncertainty is the independent contribution of each modality. Resolving this single question reframes the entire remaining search (which encoder to improve, whether fusion matters, whether multi-profile aggregation is needed) and prevents misallocating limited budget on the wrong axis.

Evidence: The multimodal setup with pca_n2000 + resnet50 (config_016, acc=0.527) outperforms RNA-only (config_001, acc=0.485) by ~4%, and concat fusion marginally beats weighted (0.527 vs 0.523). Image-only is very weak (0.208), confirming the image modality contributes little standalone but may add complementary signal in fusion. The major untested dimension is profile_setting: all completed experiments used singleprofile, so we have no evidence on whether aggregating multiple profiles per cell improves representations. Question tested: Does multiprofile aggregation (via avgpool) on top of the current best multimodal pipeline (pca_n2000 + resnet50 + concat) yield a meaningful accuracy gain over the singleprofile baseline? Why this is the best next experiment: It is the most logical exploitation of the strongest-performing direction while simultaneously resolving the largest remaining uncertainty (profile setting). Using avgpool keeps the aggregation simple and low-risk, and concat is retained as the slightly preferred fusion from prior evidence. If multiprofile helps, it opens a high-value axis for further refinement (e.g., transformer aggregation, different encoders); if it does not, we efficiently rule out an entire block of 20+ multiprofile configurations, saving budget for RNA-encoder exploration.

Evidence: The largest performance gain so far comes from switching to multi-profile with avgpool aggregation in the multimodal setting (config_018: 0.619 vs config_016: 0.527, a ~9% jump). However, we cannot yet decompose whether this gain is driven by aggregating multiple RNA profiles, multiple image profiles, or an interaction between the two. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether multi-profile benefits are modality-specific or general, which would fundamentally change where to focus remaining budget (RNA encoder quality vs. image aggregation strategy). This experiment (RNA-only, multi-profile, PCA, avgpool) directly isolates the RNA multi-profile effect: if it also shows a large gain over config_001 (0.485), the benefit is a general data-volume effect and we should prioritize encoder quality; if the gain is small, the multi-profile advantage is specific to image profile aggregation and we should invest in image encoder and aggregation choices. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most important design axis discovered so far, making all subsequent experiments more targeted under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the clear best at 0.619 acc, showing that multiprofile aggregation and multimodal fusion both contribute meaningfully. However, the only aggregation method tested so far is avgpool; transformer aggregation remains untested in the multiprofile setting. Question: Does transformer aggregation (which can model interactions between profiles) outperform simple average pooling when combining multiple profiles in the multimodal pipeline? Why this experiment: config_020 changes exactly one variable (avgpool→transformer) from the current best, making the result cleanly interpretable. If transformer helps, it identifies a new axis of improvement and justifies further exploration; if it doesn't, it confirms avgpool sufficiency and redirects budget toward other untested dimensions (e.g., image encoder or RNA encoder). Under a limited budget, isolating the effect of aggregation on the strongest baseline is the highest-information-per-experiment choice.

The current best configuration (config_018: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat; acc=0.619) establishes that multiprofile + avgpool aggregation + concat fusion is the strongest architecture. However, the RNA encoder has only been tested as PCA (a linear method). Since RNA is the dominant signal source (RNA-only multiprofile achieves 0.591 vs image-only 0.208), the choice of RNA representation is a high-impact, unexplored design axis. Config_030 swaps only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200 (a learned nonlinear single-cell embedding) while holding all other settings at their best-known values. This cleanly isolates whether a deep learned RNA representation outperforms linear PCA in this pipeline. If scvi significantly improves over PCA, it opens a high-value exploitation path; if it performs similarly, we can rule out RNA encoder as a lever and redirect budget toward image encoder or other dimensions. This is the most informative single experiment under the limited budget because it tests the largest unexplored design choice on the primary signal modality.

Evidence: The current best is config_030 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.632. Multiprofile + avgpool + concat + scvi_n200 are all supported by the data (multiprofile >> singleprofile, avgpool > transformer, concat ≈ weighted, scvi > pca). However, the image encoder has only been tested as resnet50 in the multiprofile multimodal setting; imagenet_vit_l is completely untested. Since the image modality clearly contributes (multimodal 0.632 vs rna_only 0.591), the quality of the image representation is a major unexplored design axis. Question: Does a stronger, ViT-based image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) improve over resnet50 when all other settings are held at their known-best values? Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable extension of the current best (config_030 → config_036, only image encoder changes), making the result directly interpretable. If imagenet_vit_l helps, it opens a high-ceiling branch; if it doesn't, we efficiently rule out that entire sub-space. No other untested dimension (scgpt encoder, weighted fusion) has as much potential to shift performance given the evidence so far.

The current best (config_036, 0.7150 acc) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l with avgpool and concat. The largest single-variable gains so far came from switching the image encoder (resnet50→ViT, +8.4%) and the RNA encoder (PCA→scvi, +1.3%). However, the scgpt RNA encoder has never been tested in any experiment, making it the biggest remaining uncertainty in the design space. config_048 changes only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scgpt while holding all other settings at their empirically best values (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat). This cleanly isolates whether scgpt's generative pretraining yields a meaningfully different RNA representation than scvi's VAE. If scgpt outperforms scvi_n200, it opens a new exploitation direction; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 is near-optimal and redirects budget toward aggregation/fusion refinements. Under a limited budget, resolving this high-impact, zero-information variable is more valuable than a smaller incremental change (e.g., testing weighted fusion or transformer aggregation) whose expected effect is already partially constrained by prior evidence.
